cards.front: Three things a load balancer gives you
cards.back: Scale (add servers to add capacity), availability (dead servers are skipped) and one stable entry point for TLS, rate limits and gradual rollouts.

cards.front: Why servers behind a balancer should be stateless
cards.back: So any server can handle any request; session data lives in a shared store like Redis or the database, not one server's memory.
Sees IPs and ports and decides per connection: very fast, cheap, any protocol. Examples: AWS NLB, Maglev, IPVS.
Reads full HTTP and decides per request: path routing, TLS termination, retries, canary splits, at more CPU per request.
It ignores load, so a slow server still gets its full share and builds a queue.
Pick two servers at random and send to the less busy one. It makes the worst queue much shorter without every balancer needing global counts.
When N changes almost every key moves to a different server. Use consistent hashing instead.
Liveness asks whether the process is up; readiness asks whether it can serve right now (database reachable, caches warm). Keep readiness cheap.
On deploy or scale-in, stop sending new requests to a server but let in-flight ones finish for a grace period, often 30 seconds.
Pinning users to a server makes load uneven, and a server failure logs everyone on it out. Prefer stateless servers with a shared session store.
Cap retries (one retry, or a budget of about 10% of traffic), retry only idempotent requests, and add jittered backoff.

quiz.q: One of four servers develops a bad disk and runs 3× slower. Which algorithm keeps latency lowest?
choices: Weighted round robin with equal weights
Power of two choices or least connections
quiz.why: Load-aware choices steer traffic away from the slow server; round robin keeps feeding it.

quiz.q: Every deploy causes a short burst of 5xx errors. What is most likely missing?
quiz.why: Without draining, in-flight requests are cut off when a server is removed.

quiz.q: You need /api and /images routed to different server pools. Which balancer do you need?
quiz.why: Only an L7 balancer reads the HTTP path.

quiz.q: During a partial outage, traffic to healthy servers triples and they fall over too. What likely caused it?
choices: Health checks that were too cheap
quiz.why: Retries add load exactly when the system is struggling; cap them and add backoff.

quiz.q: Users are logged out whenever a server dies. What design change fixes this?
choices: Move sessions to a shared store like Redis and keep servers stateless
quiz.why: With shared session storage any server can serve any user.

quiz.q: A huge fleet needs to spread millions of connections cheaply across many HTTP proxies. What is the usual setup?
choices: One L7 proxy in front of everything
An L4 tier spreading connections across a fleet of L7 proxies
quiz.why: L4 forwards connections fast; the L7 fleet then routes each request.

quiz.q: Your readiness check runs a heavy database query every 2 seconds on every server. What is the risk?
quiz.why: Keep readiness checks cheap or they add meaningful load.
